patient_information: A 42-year-old British male expatriate who has lived in Malawi for 18 months. He has a family history of allergy. He had previously kept bees in the United Kingdom and been frequently stung without ill effect. However, 9 months prior to presentation, he was bitten by insects at Lake Malawi and developed an asthmatic attack that resolved spontaneously.
chief_complaint: A florid itchy rash, difficulty breathing, and a feeling of impending death on the day of admission.
history_of_present_illness: Two days prior to presentation, the patient believed he was bitten on his ankle by a tick while walking in the countryside. Twenty-four hours later, he noticed a circumscribed, painless, indurated lesion on his left ankle, accompanied by fever and arthralgia. He visited a clinic where a blood film for malaria was negative and he was treated with paracetamol. On the day of admission, he developed a widespread itchy rash, which was shortly followed by progressive difficulty in breathing and feeling faint.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is a British expatriate who has been living in Malawi for 18 months. The illness began after a suspected tick bite while walking in the countryside. Nine months previously, he experienced an asthmatic attack after insect bites at Lake Malawi. Upon further questioning, he reported visiting a national game park two weeks before his current illness, where he suffered numerous painful bites from tsetse flies.
vitals: On examination, his vital signs were: temperature 38°C, pulse rate 130 bpm, and systolic blood pressure 60 mmHg.
physical_exam: On admission, the patient was clammy and in a state of collapse with a widespread urticarial rash. He had respiratory distress and stridor. There was an indurated, circumscribed swelling on the inside of his left ankle. Chest auscultation revealed expiratory wheezes. By day 3 of hospitalization, the urticarial rash was replaced by a diffuse erythematous rash, and his face had become slightly puffy.
labs_and_diagnostics: Initial laboratory results showed a haemoglobin of 17.4 g/dL, a white cell count of 6.1 G/L (85% polymorphs, 10% lymphocytes), and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 5 mm/hour. A blood film for malaria parasites was negative, and stool and urine microscopy were also negative. A chest radiograph was normal. On day 3 of admission, a thick blood film revealed 5 to 10 trypanosomes per high power field. After starting treatment, a lumbar puncture was performed and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was found to be normal. Urine monitoring during treatment showed transient protein, casts, and white cells.
differential_diagnosis: The initial diagnosis was a possible hypersensitivity reaction to a tick bite, given the anaphylactic presentation and history of allergy. Other differentials considered included invasive helminthiasis (such as acute schistosomiasis, acute fascioliasis, and Loeffler’s syndrome) and rickettsial disease. However, the absence of eosinophilia made these less likely.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was diagnosed with anaphylactic shock and treated with 0.5ml of 1:1000 adrenaline intramuscularly with good effect. He was admitted and over the next two days received intermittent intramuscular adrenaline, intravenous hydrocortisone, and oral antihistamines for ongoing episodes of urticaria, stridor, and wheezing. On day 3, his condition changed: the respiratory symptoms ceased, the rash became diffuse and erythematous, and he developed a headache, puffy face, and a sustained fever of 38-39°C. Following the diagnosis of trypanosomiasis, he was treated with suramin, starting with a test dose and completing a total course of 5.75g. His urine was monitored for nephrotoxicity, which was observed but resolved a few weeks after treatment completion.
final_diagnosis: The patient was diagnosed with Human African Trypanosomiasis (HAT), specifically the East African form caused by Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense. The diagnosis was confirmed by the microscopic demonstration of 5 to 10 trypanosomes per high power field in a thick blood film. This was supported by the clinical evolution to fever, headache, and a diffuse rash, the recognition of the ankle lesion as a trypanosomal chancre, and the epidemiological link to numerous painful tsetse fly bites in a national game park two weeks prior. A normal CSF examination confirmed it was a first-stage infection without central nervous system involvement.
